blocks.body:
The functors $\mathrm{Hom}$ and $\otimes$ are only left or right exact ([[homological-algebra]]). Derived functors measure what they lose: from a left exact functor $F$ one builds functors $R^iF$ with $R^0F = F$ such that every short exact sequence $0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0$ gives a long exact sequence that begins $0\to F(A')\to F(A)\to F(A'')$ and continues $F(A'')\to R^1F(A')\to\cdots$, and dually left derived functors $L_iF$ of a right exact $F$. This was Cartan and Eilenberg's unification of 1956: Ext and Tor, which Baer, Čech and Eilenberg-Mac Lane had introduced separately, and the cohomology theories of groups, Lie algebras and associative algebras, all turned out to be derived functors.

This page defines derived functors through projective and injective resolutions, proves their basic properties, characterises them as universal $\delta$-functors, and shows how dimension shifting and acyclic resolutions are used to compute them. It then proves the balancing theorem, that Tor and Ext can be computed by resolving either variable, treats the derived limits $\lim^n$, and describes the settings beyond module categories (Grothendieck's axioms, derived and exact categories) in which recent papers work. Bannister's paper on derived limits compares $\lim^s$ of a sum with the sum of the $\lim^s$ through the universal property; Tang's paper on profinite and solid cohomology has to settle which resolutions exist before it can compare Ext groups. The two main examples, [[tor]] and [[ext]], have their own pages.

blocks.title: Derived functors and delta-functors
blocks.body:
Let $F$ be an additive functor between module categories (or abelian categories with enough projectives or injectives).

1. If $F$ is covariant and right exact, its left derived functors are $L_iF(A) = H_i(F(P_\bullet))$ for a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$.
2. If $F$ is covariant and left exact, its right derived functors are $R^iF(B) = H^i(F(I^\bullet))$ for an injective resolution $B\to I^\bullet$.
3. If $F$ is contravariant and left exact, such as $\mathrm{Hom}(-,N)$, its right derived functors are $R^iF(A) = H^i(F(P_\bullet))$ for a projective resolution of $A$, since $F$ turns the chain complex $P_\bullet$ into a cochain complex.

In each case the augmentation is removed before $F$ is applied. A map $f\colon A\to A'$ lifts to a chain map of resolutions, and $L_iF(f)$ is the map it induces on homology.

The comparison theorem of [[homological-algebra]] makes this well defined. Two projective resolutions $P,P'$ of $A$ admit lifts $u\colon P\to P'$, $v\colon P'\to P$ of $\mathrm{id}_A$, and $vu$, $uv$ are lifts of $\mathrm{id}_A$ like the identity maps, hence homotopic to them. An additive functor carries homotopies to homotopies (apply $F$ to $\varphi-\psi = ds+sd$), so $F(u)$ and $F(v)$ are inverse isomorphisms on homology, and the isomorphism does not depend on the choice of $u$. Independence of the lift also gives functoriality: $L_iF(gf) = L_iF(g)L_iF(f)$.

blocks.title: Basic properties of derived functors
blocks.body:
Let $F$ be right exact and covariant. Then:

1. $L_0F\cong F$.
2. $L_iF(P) = 0$ for $i>0$ when $P$ is projective.
3. A short exact sequence $0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0$ gives a natural long exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&\cdots\to L_iF(A')\to L_iF(A)\to{}\\ &\qquad L_iF(A'')\xrightarrow{\partial}L_{i-1}F(A')\to\cdots{}\\ &\qquad\to L_0F(A)\to L_0F(A'')\to0.\end{aligned}$$

The analogous statements hold for right derived functors: $R^0F\cong F$, $R^iF(I) = 0$ for injective $I$ (or $R^iF(P) = 0$ for projective $P$ in the contravariant case), and a long exact sequence that starts $0\to F(A')\to F(A)\to F(A'')$ and continues $F(A'')\to R^1F(A')\to\cdots$.

1. Applying the right exact $F$ to $P_1\to P_0\to A\to0$ gives an exact $F(P_1)\to F(P_0)\to F(A)\to0$, so $L_0F(A) = \operatorname{coker}(F(P_1)\to F(P_0))\cong F(A)$.

2. Take the resolution $0\to P\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}P\to0$, with $P$ in degree $0$.

3. Choose resolutions $P'_\bullet$, $P''_\bullet$ and build $P_\bullet$ by the horseshoe lemma ([[homological-algebra]]). In each degree $0\to P'_n\to P_n\to P''_n\to0$ is split (it is $P'_n\to P'_n\oplus P''_n\to P''_n$), and an additive functor preserves split exact sequences. So $0\to F(P'_\bullet)\to F(P_\bullet)\to F(P''_\bullet)\to0$ is a short exact sequence of complexes, and its long exact homology sequence is the sequence claimed; it ends with $0$ because $L_{-1}F = 0$. Naturality comes from naturality of the long exact homology sequence, together with the fact that maps of short exact sequences lift to maps of horseshoe resolutions.

blocks.title: Delta-functors and dimension shifting
blocks.body:
A (cohomological) $\delta$-functor is a sequence of additive functors $T^0, T^1, \dots$ together with connecting maps $\delta\colon T^i(A'')\to T^{i+1}(A')$ for each short exact sequence $0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0$, natural in the sequence, such that the resulting sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to T^0(A')\to T^0(A)\to T^0(A'')\xrightarrow{\delta}{}\\ &\qquad T^1(A')\to T^1(A)\to\cdots\end{aligned}$$
is exact. Right derived functors form a $\delta$-functor. It is universal (Weibel Definition 2.1.4) if every other $\delta$-functor $S$ with a map $T^0\to S^0$ receives a unique extension to a morphism of $\delta$-functors $T\to S$. Universal $\delta$-functors are unique up to unique isomorphism, and derived functors of a right exact $F$ on a category with enough projectives are universal (Weibel 2.4.7; dually for right derived functors). Bannister's paper quotes the resulting uniqueness of derived functors as its Fact 3.26, and in Lemma 3.27 uses the universal property to compare $\lim^s$ of a sum of systems with the sum of the $\lim^s$.

Dimension shifting is the computation that makes this work. If $0\to A\to I\to C\to0$ is exact with $I$ injective, the long exact sequence of $R^\bullet F$ and $R^iF(I) = 0$ give
$$\begin{gathered}R^1F(A)\cong\operatorname{coker}\big(F(I)\to F(C)\big),\\ R^{i+1}F(A)\cong R^iF(C)\quad(i\ge1).\end{gathered}$$
So a question about $R^{i+1}F$ of one module becomes a question about $R^iF$ of another.

blocks.title: Characterisation of derived functors
blocks.body: Let $F$ be left exact, and let $(T^i,\delta)$ be a $\delta$-functor with an isomorphism $T^0\cong F$ and with $T^i(I) = 0$ for every injective $I$ and every $i>0$. Then $T^i\cong R^iF$ for all $i$, compatibly with the connecting maps. (Arapura's Theorem 5.22 states the more general version where $T^i$ is only required to be effaceable: every $A$ embeds in some $B$ with $T^i(A)\to T^i(B)$ zero.)

Both $T$ and $R^\bullet F$ satisfy the dimension shifting formulas above, because those were derived only from the long exact sequence and vanishing on injectives. Choose for each $A$ an embedding $0\to A\to I\to C\to0$ into an injective. Then
$$T^1(A)\cong\operatorname{coker}(F(I)\to F(C))\cong R^1F(A),$$
and inductively $T^{i+1}(A)\cong T^i(C)\cong R^iF(C)\cong R^{i+1}F(A)$. One checks that these isomorphisms do not depend on the chosen embedding (two embeddings are dominated by a third, $A\to I\oplus I'$) and are natural in $A$ (a map $A\to A'$ extends to the chosen injectives by injectivity) and compatible with $\delta$. These checks are routine diagram chases and are not written out here; Arapura's Theorem 5.22 states the result in the effaceable generality, Wikipedia's article on derived functors gives the same characterisation by vanishing on injectives, and Bannister quotes it as his Fact 3.26.

blocks.title: Acyclic resolutions
blocks.body:
It is often convenient to resolve by objects that are not projective but are invisible to the derived functors. An object $Q$ is $F$-acyclic if $L_iF(Q) = 0$ for all $i>0$. If $Q_\bullet\to A$ is a resolution by $F$-acyclic objects, then $L_iF(A)\cong H_i(F(Q_\bullet))$.

Proof by dimension shifting (Weibel Exercise 2.4.3), by induction on $i$ simultaneously for all modules that have an acyclic resolution. For $i = 0$ this is right exactness of $F$. Let $K = \ker(Q_0\to A)$; the truncated complex $Q_{\ge1}$, reindexed down by one, is an acyclic resolution of $K$. The long exact sequence of $0\to K\to Q_0\to A\to0$ and acyclicity of $Q_0$ give $L_1F(A)\cong\ker(F(K)\to F(Q_0))$ and $L_{i+1}F(A)\cong L_iF(K)$ for $i\ge1$. Since $Q_2\to Q_1\to K\to0$ is exact and $F$ is right exact, $F(K) = F(Q_1)/\operatorname{im}F(Q_2)$, so
$$\begin{aligned}&\ker(F(K)\to F(Q_0))\\ &\quad= \ker(F(Q_1)\to F(Q_0))/\operatorname{im}F(Q_2)\\ &\quad= H_1(F(Q_\bullet)).\end{aligned}$$
For $i\ge1$ the induction hypothesis applied to $K$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}L_{i+1}F(A)&\cong L_iF(K)\cong H_i(F(Q_{\ge1+\bullet}))\\ &= H_{i+1}(F(Q_\bullet)).\end{aligned}$$

The main instance is Weibel's flat resolution lemma: flat modules are acyclic for $-\otimes B$ (shown on the [[tor]] page), so Tor can be computed from flat resolutions. Another: Bannister uses that injective inverse systems are acyclic for $\lim$ (his Corollary 3.23).

blocks.title: Dimension shifting in action
blocks.body: Over $R = \mathbb{Z}/4$, let $F = -\otimes_R\mathbb{Z}/2$. Compute $L_iF(\mathbb{Z}/2)$ for all $i$ using only the short exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ and dimension shifting.
blocks.solution:
The middle term $R = \mathbb{Z}/4$ is free, so $L_iF(R) = 0$ for $i>0$, and the long exact sequence gives
$$0\to L_1F(\mathbb{Z}/2)\to F(\mathbb{Z}/2)\xrightarrow{F(2)}F(\mathbb{Z}/4)\to F(\mathbb{Z}/2)\to0,\qquad L_{i+1}F(\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong L_iF(\mathbb{Z}/2)\ (i\ge1).$$
Here $F(\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2\otimes_R\mathbb{Z}/2 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $F(\mathbb{Z}/4) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, and $F(2)$ is multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}/2$, which is $0$. So $L_1F(\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, and then every $L_iF(\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. These are the groups $\mathrm{Tor}_i^{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ of [[tor]]; the computation never wrote down a resolution, only one syzygy, which happened to be the module itself.

blocks.title: What a derived functor is
blocks.body: The same objects $L_iF$, $R^iF$ are described in four ways in the sources, and papers switch between them without comment.

items.label: Resolve and apply
items.body: Replace a module by a projective (or injective) resolution, apply $F$ termwise, take homology. Concrete and computable; well defined by the comparison theorem. This is the definition in Weibel, Arapura and Wikipedia, and the one used for actual calculations.

items.label: Universal delta-functor
items.body: $R^\bullet F$ is the universal way to extend $F$ to a functor that turns short exact sequences into long exact ones; it is characterised by vanishing on injectives (or effaceability). This view is what one uses to prove that two constructions agree without computing either, as Bannister does for derived limits.

items.label: Derived category
items.body: Regard a module as a complex concentrated in degree $0$ and invert quasi-isomorphisms. Then a resolution is isomorphic to the module itself, $RF$ is $F$ applied to a resolution, and $\mathrm{Ext}^i(X,Y) = \mathrm{Hom}_{D}(X,Y[i])$. This is the Stacks Project's definition and the setting of Tang's comparison of profinite and solid Ext.

items.label: Homotopy groups
items.body: An injective resolution $I^\bullet$ of $B$ gives the complex $\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet)$; shifted by $n$ and truncated to non-negative degrees, the Dold-Kan correspondence turns it into a simplicial abelian group, i.e. a space, whose $\pi_i$ is $\mathrm{Ext}^{n-i}(A,B)$ for $0\le i\le n$. In particular $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)$ is $\pi_0$ of the space of maps from (a resolution of) $A$ into the shifted object $B[n]$, which nLab writes as the $n$-fold delooping of $B$. A reply in the r/math thread recommends this picture to someone who saw Ext as mere diagram chasing.

blocks.body:
1. Show that if $F$ is exact then $L_iF = 0$ for $i>0$.
2. Let $0\to K\to P\to A\to0$ with $P$ projective. Show $L_{i+1}F(A)\cong L_iF(K)$ for $i\ge1$. Use this to show that $L_iF(A) = 0$ for $i>n$ if $A$ has a projective resolution of length $n$.
3. Show that a direct summand of an $F$-acyclic object is $F$-acyclic, and that $L_iF$ commutes with finite direct sums.
4. Let $F = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/n,-)$. Compute $R^1F(\mathbb{Z})$ from the injective resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$.

blocks.title: Balancing: resolving either variable
blocks.body:
The two basic derived functors are $\mathrm{Tor}_n(A,B) = L_n(-\otimes B)(A)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = R^n\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)(A)$, the subjects of [[tor]] and [[ext]]. Both are defined by resolving the first variable, and both pages use the balancing isomorphism that lets one resolve the second instead. This section proves it. The tool is the double complex. A (first-quadrant) double complex is a family of modules $C_{p,q}$, $p,q\ge0$, with horizontal maps $d^h\colon C_{p,q}\to C_{p-1,q}$ and vertical maps $d^v\colon C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1}$ such that $(d^h)^2 = 0$, $(d^v)^2 = 0$ and $d^hd^v+d^vd^h = 0$. Its total complex has $\mathrm{Tot}(C)_n = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}$ and differential $d = d^h+d^v$; the anticommutation gives $d^2 = 0$. If the squares commute instead, one inserts the sign $(-1)^p$ on the vertical maps (the sign trick of the conventions table).

The example that matters: for chain complexes $P_\bullet$ and $Q_\bullet$, the tensor double complex $C_{p,q} = P_p\otimes Q_q$ with $d^h = d\otimes1$ and $d^v = (-1)^p\,1\otimes d$. Weibel's Theorem 2.7.2 proves balance with the acyclic assembly lemma (his Lemma 2.7.3) and the mapping cone of the augmentation, and Boe's course follows the same route; that is the proof given here. The Michigan notes on Tor instead use a lemma about double complexes whose rows and columns are all exact.

blocks.title: Indexing and double complexes
blocks.body: Sources agree on the mathematics but not on the bookkeeping. Before reading a paper, check these.

rows.text: Right derived functors and Ext carry upper (cohomological) indices, $R^iF$, $\mathrm{Ext}^i$; left derived functors and Tor carry lower (homological) indices, $L_iF$, $\mathrm{Tor}_i$. Long exact sequences of Ext climb in index, those of Tor descend.

Horizontal and vertical differentials anticommute, $d^hd^v+d^vd^h = 0$, and the total differential is $d^h+d^v$ (Weibel 1.2.4-1.2.6). Commuting squares are turned into anticommuting ones by the sign trick, replacing $d^v_{p,q}$ by $(-1)^pd^v_{p,q}$; for $P\otimes Q$ this gives $d^v = (-1)^p\,1\otimes d$ (Weibel 2.7.1).
Keeps the squares commuting and puts the sign into the total complex: $d = \sum_{p+q=n}\big(d_1^{p,q}+(-1)^pd_2^{p,q}\big)$ (Definition 12.18.3). The two conventions give isomorphic total complexes.

blocks.title: Exact columns give an exact total complex
blocks.body: Let $C$ be a double complex with $C_{p,q} = 0$ unless $p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$, and suppose that every column $(C_{p,\bullet},d^v)$ is exact. Then $\mathrm{Tot}(C)$ is exact. (This is the first-quadrant case of Weibel's acyclic assembly Lemma 2.7.3.)

Let $x = (x_{n,0},x_{n-1,1},\dots,x_{0,n})\in\mathrm{Tot}_n$ be a cycle, with $x_{p,q}\in C_{p,q}$. Being a cycle means that for each $p+q = n-1$,
$$d^hx_{p+1,q}+d^vx_{p,q+1} = 0.$$
We remove the components one at a time, starting from the bottom row. Column $n$ is exact at $q = 0$, so $d^v\colon C_{n,1}\to C_{n,0}$ is onto, and $x_{n,0} = d^vy_{n,1}$. Replace $x$ by $x-d(y_{n,1})$; this changes $x$ only in positions $(n,0)$ and $(n-1,1)$, kills the first, and is still a cycle in the same homology class. Now $x_{n,0} = 0$, and the cycle condition at $(n-1,0)$ reads $d^vx_{n-1,1} = 0$. Column $n-1$ is exact at $q = 1$, so $x_{n-1,1} = d^vy_{n-1,2}$; subtract $d(y_{n-1,2})$, which kills the $(n-1,1)$ component and only changes $(n-2,2)$ further. Continue along the anti-diagonal. After $n+1$ steps all components are zero, so the original $x$ was $d$ of the sum of the $y$'s. The process stops because the double complex lives in the first quadrant: there are only $n+1$ components to kill.

blocks.caption: The staircase argument. A cycle in total degree n has one component on each square of the anti-diagonal. Exactness of the columns lets one kill the component on the bottom row by a vertical boundary, which only disturbs the next square up and to the left, and so on to the top.
blocks.alt: A grid of dots for a first-quadrant double complex with p horizontal and q vertical. The anti-diagonal p plus q equals 3 is highlighted, with x components at (3,0), (2,1), (1,2), (0,3). Arrows show y components one row higher being mapped down by the vertical differential and left by the horizontal one, forming a staircase from the bottom right to the top left.

blocks.title: Balancing Tor and Ext
blocks.body:
Let $P_\bullet\to A$ be a projective resolution of a right module and $Q_\bullet\to B$ one of a left module. The augmentations induce quasi-isomorphisms
$$P_\bullet\otimes B\ \xleftarrow{\ \simeq\ }\ \mathrm{Tot}(P_\bullet\otimes Q_\bullet)\ \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }\ A\otimes Q_\bullet.$$
Hence $H_n(P_\bullet\otimes B)\cong H_n(A\otimes Q_\bullet)$: Tor may be computed by resolving either variable. For $R$ commutative, $P_p\otimes Q_q\cong Q_q\otimes P_p$ gives $\mathrm{Tor}_n(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n(B,A)$. Dually, for a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ and an injective resolution $B\to I^\bullet$, the cochain complexes $\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet,B)$, $\mathrm{Tot}\,\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet,I^\bullet)$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet)$ are quasi-isomorphic, so the two definitions of Ext agree (Weibel 2.7.2 and 2.7.6).

Two facts: a chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if its mapping cone is exact (exercises of the complexes section of [[homological-algebra]], from the long exact sequence of $0\to D\to\operatorname{cone}\to C[-1]\to0$), and exact columns give an exact total complex.

Let $\varepsilon\colon\mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)\to P\otimes B$ be $1\otimes\eta$ on the bottom row $P_p\otimes Q_0$ and zero elsewhere, where $\eta\colon Q_0\to B$ is the augmentation. Form a new double complex $D$ by adding the row $D_{p,-1} = P_p\otimes B$ below $P\otimes Q$, with vertical maps $(-1)^p\,1\otimes\eta\colon P_p\otimes Q_0\to P_p\otimes B$. The $p$-th column of $D$ is $P_p\otimes(\cdots\to Q_1\to Q_0\to B\to0)$. This is exact: $P_p$ is projective, hence flat, and the augmented resolution is exact. After moving the row index up by one, $D$ is a first-quadrant double complex with exact columns, so $\mathrm{Tot}(D)$ is exact. But
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Tot}(D)_n &= \bigoplus_{p+q=n}P_p\otimes Q_q\ \oplus\ P_{n+1}\otimes B\\ &= \mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)_n\oplus(P\otimes B)_{n+1},\end{aligned}$$
and comparing differentials shows that $\mathrm{Tot}(D)$ is the mapping cone of $\varepsilon$, shifted by one degree and with signs changed on some summands (which affects neither exactness). So the cone of $\varepsilon$ is exact and $\varepsilon$ is a quasi-isomorphism. The same argument with rows instead of columns (each row $(\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to A\to0)\otimes Q_q$ is exact because $Q_q$ is flat) gives the other quasi-isomorphism.

For commutativity, the map $P_p\otimes Q_q\to Q_q\otimes P_p$, $x\otimes y\mapsto(-1)^{pq}y\otimes x$ is an isomorphism of total complexes, and the right side computes $\mathrm{Tor}(B,A)$ by the first part. The Ext statement is proved by the same steps with $\mathrm{Hom}(P_p,I^q)$: the columns $\mathrm{Hom}(P_p,B\to I^\bullet)$ are exact because $\mathrm{Hom}(P_p,-)$ is exact, and the rows $\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet\to A,I^q)$ are exact because $\mathrm{Hom}(-,I^q)$ is exact.

blocks.title: The total complex in the smallest case
blocks.body: Over $\mathbb{Z}$, take $P = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{4}\mathbb{Z})\to\mathbb{Z}/4$ and $Q = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{6}\mathbb{Z})\to\mathbb{Z}/6$. Write down $\mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)$ and compute its homology.
blocks.solution:
All four terms $P_p\otimes Q_q$ are $\mathbb{Z}$. In degree $2$ there is $P_1\otimes Q_1$, in degree $1$ the sum $P_0\otimes Q_1\oplus P_1\otimes Q_0$, in degree $0$ the term $P_0\otimes Q_0$. With $d^h = 4$ and $d^v = (-1)^p\,6$:
$$\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ e\mapsto(4,\,-6)\ }\mathbb{Z}^2\xrightarrow{\ (u,v)\mapsto 6u+4v\ }\mathbb{Z}.$$
The composite is $24-24 = 0$. $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}/(6,4) = \mathbb{Z}/2 = \mathbb{Z}/4\otimes\mathbb{Z}/6$. The kernel of $(u,v)\mapsto6u+4v$ is generated by $(2,-3)$, and the image of the first map is generated by $(4,-6) = 2(2,-3)$, so $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2 = \mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/4,\mathbb{Z}/6)$. The first map is injective, so $H_2 = 0$. Resolving only $\mathbb{Z}/4$ gives $\mathbb{Z}/6\xrightarrow{4}\mathbb{Z}/6$, and resolving only $\mathbb{Z}/6$ gives $\mathbb{Z}/4\xrightarrow{6}\mathbb{Z}/4$; both have the same homology $\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2$, as the theorem says.

blocks.title: Why the two resolutions agree
blocks.body: Balancing is the first theorem in the subject that is not a formal consequence of the definitions, and each source proves it differently.

items.label: Cone and assembly
items.body: Show that the augmentation $\mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)\to P\otimes B$ has exact mapping cone, because the cone is the total complex of a double complex with exact columns (acyclic assembly). This is Weibel's proof of Theorem 2.7.2, which Boe's course follows and which is given above.

items.label: Acyclic double complex
items.body: Prove once that for a first-quadrant double complex whose rows and columns are exact except at the edge, the homology of the bottom row, of the left column and of the total complex all coincide; apply it to $P\otimes Q$. This is how the Michigan notes on Tor organise the argument.

items.label: Two spectral sequences
items.body: Filter the total complex by rows or by columns; each filtration gives a spectral sequence converging to $H(\mathrm{Tot})$, and when one family of lines is exact the spectral sequence collapses. nLab describes balanced Tor this way, and Holanda-Miranda-Neto use the same two spectral sequences on a Hom-tensor double complex to obtain Ext-Tor dualities and five-term exact sequences.

items.label: Derived category
items.body: In $D(R)$ a resolution is isomorphic to the module it resolves, so the derived tensor product $A\otimes^LB$ may be computed by replacing either or both arguments; balance becomes the statement that $P\otimes Q\to P\otimes B$ is a quasi-isomorphism when $P$ is a complex of flat modules.

blocks.body:
1. Check that $d = d^h+d^v$ squares to zero on $\mathrm{Tot}(C)$ when $d^hd^v+d^vd^h = 0$, and that the sign trick turns a commuting double complex into an anticommuting one.
2. Give an example of a double complex in the second quadrant (unbounded) with exact columns whose direct-sum total complex is not exact. Where does the staircase argument break?
3. Use balance and the resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$ in the second variable to compute $\mathrm{Tor}_1(A,\mathbb{Z}/n)$ for any abelian group $A$.
4. Use the balancing theorem to derive the long exact Tor sequence in the second variable from the one in the first.

blocks.title: Derived limits
blocks.body:
The inverse limit of a tower $A_0\xleftarrow{f_1}A_1\xleftarrow{f_2}A_2\leftarrow\cdots$ of abelian groups is the kernel of
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta\colon\prod_iA_i\to\prod_iA_i,\\ \Delta(a_i)_i = \big(a_i-f_{i+1}(a_{i+1})\big)_i,\end{gathered}$$
and Weibel defines $\lim^1A_i = \operatorname{coker}\Delta$ (Definition 3.5.1). The functor $\lim$ is left exact but not exact, and $\lim^1$ measures the failure; Weibel sets $\lim^n = 0$ for $n\ge2$ on towers and shows that $\lim,\lim^1$ form a $\delta$-functor (Lemma 3.5.2) and that on towers they are the right derived functors of $\lim$ (Corollary 3.5.4). For inverse systems indexed by larger posets (Bannister works over $\omega^\kappa$), the higher derived functors $\lim^n$ need not vanish; Bannister's paper studies exactly these higher derived limits, computes them through an explicit alternating cochain complex whose $n$-th cohomology is $\lim^n$ (his Definition 3.5 and Proposition 3.7), and draws consequences for strong homology.

blocks.title: The lim-lim^1 sequence
blocks.body:
Let $0\to(A_i)\to(B_i)\to(C_i)\to0$ be a short exact sequence of towers (exact at each $i$, with compatible maps). Then there is an exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\lim A_i\to\lim B_i\to\lim C_i\to{}\\ &\qquad\lim{}^1A_i\to\lim{}^1B_i\to\lim{}^1C_i\to0.\end{aligned}$$
If all maps $f_i$ of a tower are surjective, its $\lim^1$ is zero (Weibel Lemma 3.5.3); more generally $\lim^1 = 0$ for towers satisfying the Mittag-Leffler condition, that the images of $A_{i+k}\to A_i$ stabilise for each $i$ (Weibel Proposition 3.5.7, not proved here).

Products of short exact sequences of abelian groups are exact, so $0\to\prod A_i\to\prod B_i\to\prod C_i\to0$ is exact, and $\Delta$ acts compatibly on the three products. The snake lemma ([[homological-algebra]]) applied to $\Delta$ gives exactly the six-term sequence, since $\lim = \ker\Delta$ and $\lim^1 = \operatorname{coker}\Delta$; the outer zeros come from the injectivity and surjectivity addenda of the snake lemma.

If every $f_i$ is surjective and $(b_i)\in\prod A_i$, solve $a_i-f_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = b_i$ recursively: put $a_0 = 0$, and having $a_i$ choose $a_{i+1}$ with $f_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = a_i-b_i$. Then $\Delta(a) = b$, so $\Delta$ is onto.

blocks.title: A non-zero lim^1
blocks.body: Compute $\lim$ and $\lim^1$ of the tower $\mathbb{Z}\xleftarrow{p}\mathbb{Z}\xleftarrow{p}\mathbb{Z}\leftarrow\cdots$.
blocks.solution:
The tower is isomorphic to the tower of subgroups $\mathbb{Z}\supseteq p\mathbb{Z}\supseteq p^2\mathbb{Z}\supseteq\cdots$ with inclusions ($p^i\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}$ via division by $p^i$). Consider the short exact sequence of towers
$$0\to(p^i\mathbb{Z})_i\to(\mathbb{Z})_i\to(\mathbb{Z}/p^i)_i\to0,$$
where the middle tower is constant with identity maps and the right-hand one has the reduction maps. The constant tower has $\lim = \mathbb{Z}$ and $\lim^1 = 0$ (its maps are onto); the tower $\mathbb{Z}/p^i$ has surjective maps, so $\lim^1 = 0$, and $\lim = \mathbb{Z}_p$, the $p$-adic integers; and $\lim p^i\mathbb{Z} = \bigcap_ip^i\mathbb{Z} = 0$. The six-term sequence becomes
$$0\to0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}_p\to\lim{}^1(p^i\mathbb{Z})\to0\to0\to0,$$
so $\lim^1 = \mathbb{Z}_p/\mathbb{Z}$, an uncountable group, although every group in the tower is $\mathbb{Z}$. In topology this is why the Milnor sequence $0\to\lim^1H^{q-1}(X_i)\to H^q(X)\to\lim H^q(X_i)\to0$ for an increasing union of subcomplexes (Weibel Application 3.5.9) can have a large correction term.

blocks.body:
1. Show that $\lim^1 = 0$ for a tower of finite groups. (Weibel Exercise 3.5.2; verify Mittag-Leffler.)
2. Prove that Mittag-Leffler implies $\lim^1 = 0$ when all the stable images are attained after one step, i.e. $\operatorname{im}(A_{i+k}\to A_i) = \operatorname{im}(A_{i+1}\to A_i)$ for all $k\ge1$.
3. Compute $\lim$ and $\lim^1$ of $\mathbb{Z}\xleftarrow{n_1}\mathbb{Z}\xleftarrow{n_2}\mathbb{Z}\leftarrow\cdots$ for an arbitrary sequence of integers $n_i\ge2$.
4. Show that $\lim^1$ of a tower of surjections of chain complexes vanishes degreewise, and deduce the short exact sequence relating $H(\lim C_i)$ to $\lim H(C_i)$ and $\lim^1H(C_i)$ in that case (compare Weibel Theorem 3.5.8).

blocks.title: Beyond modules: Grothendieck's axioms, derived and exact categories
blocks.body:
Three generalisations appear in the papers, and the page now has the vocabulary to state them.

1. Grothendieck's axioms. In an abelian category, AB3 asks that all coproducts exist, AB4 that coproducts of short exact sequences are exact, and AB5 that filtered colimits are exact; AB3* and AB4* are the dual conditions for products. Modules satisfy AB5 and AB4*, but not AB5*: inverse limits are not exact, and the failure is exactly $\lim^1$. Tang's paper checks which axioms hold for profinite and solid modules (its Sections 1-2), because derived functors and the comparison of Ext groups depend on them. The Stacks Project discusses the relevant property for products in its Section 12.32.
2. Derived categories. The derived category $D(\mathcal{A})$ has complexes as objects and inverts quasi-isomorphisms. Then $\mathrm{Ext}^i(X,Y) = \mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[i])$ for all complexes, the long exact Ext sequences come from distinguished triangles, and Yoneda Ext and derived Ext are identified (Stacks Section 13.27). Tang defers this to his Section 4. This page only uses the phrase; the subject belongs to a later page.
3. Exact categories and relative homological algebra. In Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson's formulation (their Definition 3.2, equivalent to Quillen's axioms), an exact structure on an abelian category is a class $\mathcal{E}$ of short exact sequences, the 'admissible' ones, closed under isomorphism, such that identities are admissible monos and epis, admissible monos and admissible epis are closed under composition, admissible monos are stable under pushout along any map, and admissible epis are stable under pullback along any map. The split sequences form the smallest exact structure and all short exact sequences the largest. On a general additive category one asks the same of a class of kernel-cokernel pairs. Restricting to a smaller class of short exact sequences on a module category gives relative projectives (objects $P$ with $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ exact on admissible sequences) and a relative $\mathrm{Ext}^1$, the classes of admissible extensions inside $\mathrm{Ext}^1$; the paper's Remark 3.6 describes an exact structure as a closed additive subbifunctor of $\mathrm{Ext}^1(-,-)$, so these classes form a subgroup under Baer sum. This is the framework of Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson, who choose exact structures on persistence modules so that minimal relative projective resolutions give homological invariants such as relative Betti numbers and the rank invariant. Their Grothendieck groups and Krull-Remak-Schmidt decompositions are not covered here.

1. Show that in the category of abelian groups, a product of short exact sequences is exact (AB4*), but that the inverse limit of the short exact sequences $0\to p^i\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/p^i\to0$ is not exact.
2. Show that the split short exact sequences form an exact structure on any additive category, and that every object is relatively projective for it.
3. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the class of short exact sequences of abelian groups on which every functor $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/m,-)$ is exact. Show that each $\mathbb{Z}/m$ is relatively projective for $\mathcal{E}$, that $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ is not in $\mathcal{E}$, and that the classes in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,A)$ of sequences in $\mathcal{E}$ form a subgroup.

blocks.title: Reading the papers
blocks.body:
Here is where each paper's prerequisites from this page are treated.

1. Holanda and Miranda-Neto, Cohen-Macaulay Burch rings. Double complexes and the two spectral sequences of a Hom-tensor double complex (balancing, and the views on why the two resolutions agree; spectral sequences proper are on the [[spectral-sequences]] page). The Ext-Tor dualities they produce are on [[ext]].
2. Blanchette, Brüstle and Hanson, exact structures for persistence modules. Exact structures and relative Ext (beyond modules). Not here: almost split sequences, representation dimension, Grothendieck groups.
3. Tang, profinite and solid cohomology. Grothendieck's AB axioms and the derived category (beyond modules), and the derived-category reading of a derived functor (the views on what a derived functor is). Yoneda Ext and group cohomology are on [[ext]].
4. Bannister, derived limits in the Cohen model. Inverse systems, left exactness of $\lim$, $\lim^n$ as derived functors and the lim-lim^1 sequence (derived limits), acyclicity and the uniqueness of universal $\delta$-functors (derived functors and delta-functors). Not here: the set theory.

This page builds on [[homological-algebra]]: resolutions, the comparison theorem, the horseshoe lemma and the long exact homology sequence. The derived functors of $\otimes$ and $\mathrm{Hom}$ are [[tor]] and [[ext]], which use the balancing theorem proved here. [[sheaf-cohomology]] is the right derived functor of global sections, computed by injective or acyclic resolutions exactly as here, and [[spectral-sequences]] start from the double complexes of the balancing section. The Milnor sequence of the derived limits section reappears in [[cohomology]], and the adjunction arguments are instances of [[yoneda-adjunctions]].
